findings.source_passage: in those jaws of swift destruction, like another cursed Jonah (by which name indeed they called him), bustles a little withered old man, who, for their money, dearly sells the sailors deliriums and death
findings.why_it_matters: The draft renders this as 'another cursed Jonah who, for their money, dearly sells the sailors deliriums and death' — stripping the parenthetical '(by which name indeed they called him)' which is part of the rhetorical texture, and losing the build-up through the whale-jaw description that makes the Jonah conceit land. The phrase 'deliriums and death' survives but its syntactic framing is compressed.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the fuller sentence structure including the parenthetical '(by which name indeed they called him)' and the preceding detail about 'old decanters, bottles, flasks' to preserve the full gothic-comic buildup.

findings.source_passage: The more I pondered over this harpooneer, the more I abominated the thought of sleeping with him... I began to twitch all over... Suppose now, he should tumble in upon me at midnight—how could I tell from what vile hole he had been coming?
findings.source_locator: paragraphs of Ishmael's anxious deliberation before demanding the bench
findings.why_it_matters: This sustained comic-anxious interior monologue — including 'I began to twitch all over' and 'from what vile hole he had been coming' — is pure voice-establishing material. The draft jumps directly from the 'no man prefers to sleep two in a bed' paragraph to 'I declared I'd try the bench,' erasing the escalating paranoia that gives the scene its comic engine.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'I abominated the thought' paragraph with at least the key lines about the harpooneer's potentially untidy linen, the twitching, and the midnight speculation — these are the comic texture the scene depends on.

findings.source_passage: "may be not," taking out a stick and whittling a toothpick, "but I rayther guess you'll be done brown if that ere harpooneer hears you a slanderin' his head." "I'll break it for him," said I... "It's broke a'ready," said he.
findings.source_locator: the landlord-and-Ishmael dialogue about the head, middle of chapter
findings.why_it_matters: The full comic escalation of this exchange — the whittling toothpick, 'done brown,' 'I'll break it for him,' 'It's broke a'ready' — is the funniest sustained dialogue in the chapter. The draft compresses this entire back-and-forth to a single sentence, erasing the deadpan wit that is one of Melville's most celebrated comic passages.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the key beats of this exchange: the landlord's whittling, the 'done brown' line, Ishmael's 'I'll break it,' and the landlord's 'It's broke a'ready' rejoinder — these are critically recognized as signature comic prose.

findings.source_passage: "Depend upon it, landlord, that harpooneer is a dangerous man." "He pays reg'lar," was the rejoinder.
findings.source_locator: after the New Zealand heads explanation
findings.why_it_matters: This two-line exchange is one of the most quoted comic deflations in Melville — the moral concern instantly neutralized by commercial practicality. Its absence removes a key moment of satirical voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore both lines verbatim; they are brief enough to include without budget pressure.

findings.source_passage: It was cold as Iceland—no fire at all—the landlord said he couldn't afford it. Nothing but two dismal tallow candles, each in a winding sheet. We were fain to button up our monkey jackets, and hold to our lips cups of scalding tea with our half frozen fingers.
findings.why_it_matters: The draft preserves 'two dismal tallow candles, each in a winding sheet' and the dumplings but drops 'cold as Iceland,' the monkey jackets, and the scalding tea with half-frozen fingers — the sensory accumulation that makes the scene vivid.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'cold as Iceland—no fire at all' and the monkey-jacket/scalding-tea detail to maintain the atmospheric texture.

findings.source_passage: his very legs were marked, as if a parcel of dark green frogs were running up the trunks of young palms
findings.why_it_matters: This simile is distinctive and memorable — one of the more striking figurative flourishes in Queequeg's introduction. The draft notes the legs were marked but drops the simile entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the frog/palm simile when describing Queequeg's tattooed legs.

summary: The draft preserves the chapter's skeleton and several key set-pieces but erases multiple voice-defining passages: the full landlord-Ishmael comic exchange about the broken head (including 'done brown' and 'He pays reg'lar'), Ishmael's anxious pre-bench interior monologue, and several rhetorically distinctive details — together constituting three medium-severity failures that trigger regeneration.
